Meeting header
Date: 2025-11-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Wong (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Bridgeway), Samir Rao (Bridgeway), Jules Ortega (Bridgeway Security), Priya Nair (Bridgeway Dev)

Summary:
Quick developer handoff covering Python/TypeScript SDK integration, auth patterns (API key vs SSO), sandbox environment setup, brief Console/Optimize walkthrough, and next steps to run a short latency pilot. Security questions raised about KMS + audit logs. Agreed to pilot and exchange sandbox creds + benchmarks.

Topics:

- Environment variables, CI secrets, rotation
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) for regulated data

Transcript body:
00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, AE for Redwood Inference. Today Ethan and I will run through the SDK quickstart for Python and TS, show the console a quick optimization flow, and then go over how you'd run a short latency pilot.
00:11 Speaker 2 (Ethan): morning all, quick note our demo environment is a sandbox with a small dedicated pool; we can mirror your QPS in the pilot.
00:20 Speaker 3 (Laura): awesome, thanks. main goals: low p95 latency for our realtime fraud checks, keys must not leave region, and compliance needs a KMS-backed key.
00:33 Speaker 1 (Maya): got it. we'll cover KMS options - hosted can use customer CMK in KMS, and Private has on-prem KMS hooks.
00:42 Speaker 2 (Ethan): quick architecture note: SDK calls hit the Red API gateway, routing policy decides host vs dedicated, we can pin a model version. also default SDK does transparently handle streaming and KV cache for responses.
01:03 Speaker 4 (Samir): when you say KV cache, do you mean key-value cache on the server? we need to ensure it's not persisting PII.
01:12 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yeah, good question. clarify: prefix/KV cache is in-memory on serving runtime and not persisted unless you opt into caching. for Private we can set retention to zero; for Hosted we can sign a data handling agreement and enable ephemeral caches. sorry if I said K-V cash earlier, the transcription is weird.
01:34 Speaker 5 (Jules): security: SOC2 and audit logs, can we get the full audit schema and retention options?
01:42 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, we'll send the SOC2 pack; audit logs are per-tenant and you can push them to your SIEM via S3/Logstream. we'll include retention config.
01:51 Speaker 3 (Laura): perfect. show us the SDK steps — we plan to integrate in a Node service and a Python worker.
02:00 Speaker 2 (Ethan): demo time. first the Python quickstart — we have an official package 'redwood-inference' on PyPI. typical flow: pip install redwood-inference, export REDWOOD_API_KEY env var, then client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY")) and client.generate(...)
02:30 Speaker 3 (Laura): what about SSO or service accounts? we use SAML with Okta; secrets need rotation every 90 days.
02:40 Speaker 2 (Ethan): you can bind team SSO to the console and mint short-lived API keys tied to identities; for CI we recommend using a service token with limited scope and rotate via KMS/GHA. we'll also send a GitHub Actions snippet showing auto-rotation.
03:01 Speaker 6 (Priya): for TypeScript, what's the snippet?
03:06 Speaker 2 (Ethan): npm i @redwood/inference, then in code new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }) — same shape as Python. types are provided. we have streaming examples for websocket and SSE and also sample code for incremental KV cache reuse.
03:31 Speaker 4 (Samir): do you provide typed mocks for local dev? our CI wants deterministic tests.
03:36 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes, we supply a local mock server (redwood-mock) that supports recorded responses; you can run it with docker compose. will add link.
03:48 Speaker 3 (Laura): how about local env switching across staging/prod?
03:52 Speaker 1 (Maya): Console supports multiple API tokens and envs; we recommend prefixing env vars like REDWOOD_API_KEY_STAGING and REDWOOD_API_KEY_PROD and using a small wrapper loader. there's a sample repo we'll share.
04:12 Speaker 2 (Ethan): moving on, Console quick tour — route config, per-model cost breakdown, token-level latency. this helps tune batch sizes and dedupe caching.
04:27 Speaker 5 (Jules): can we restrict which teams see cost data?
04:30 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes RBAC lets you set role-level views; we'll show screenshots after.
04:36 Speaker 3 (Laura): about Dedicated: we have regulatory requirements to keep data within AWS eu-west-1 and tight network controls. is dedicated enough or do we need Private?
04:46 Speaker 2 (Ethan): Dedicated gives a reserved GPU pool you control via API, and you can restrict egress; it's usually enough but if you need a private control plane and VPC peering in your own account, Private (VPC/on-prem) is the path. we can do a hybrid—dedicated in your VPC for strict controls.
05:10 Speaker 4 (Samir): price delta? how much more is Dedicated vs Hosted?
05:16 Speaker 1 (Maya): pricing bands depend on committed spend. we'll provide an estimate and example compute bands. Sales Ops will send the committed capacity estimate after they see your expected QPS.
05:28 Speaker 6 (Priya): Optimize — what do we get out of the box to reduce cost?
05:33 Speaker 2 (Ethan): Redwood Optimize suggests batching config, quantization profiles, and model variant suggestions per workload. for low-latency realtime we usually recommend smaller batches, prefix KV caching, and model quantization if your quality tolerates it.
05:50 Speaker 3 (Laura): can Optimize run against our prompt set?
05:54 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes, you upload eval prompts into the console and Optimize runs a recommendation job and shows predicted cost/latency tradeoffs. we'll demo that in the pilot.
06:10 Speaker 5 (Jules): audit: we need to show key rotation events mapped to user ids. doable?
06:16 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes, audit logs include token creation/rotation and the CID of the agent — we'll include an example log row in the packet.
06:28 Speaker 1 (Maya): I'm going to share a short notebook for the Python quickstart. Ethan, can you show the sample TS snippet next?
06:36 Speaker 2 (Ethan): sure. (shares code) the sample pattern is short lived client instantiation for each request to allow client side tracing; we also provide long-lived pool clients for high QPS. caveat: long-lived clients keep KV cache in memory longer which can change latency profiles.
06:58 Speaker 3 (Laura): can we test both streaming and non-streaming endpoints? streaming is important for our realtime checks.
07:05 Speaker 2 (Ethan): absolutely. streaming uses SSE by default in the SDK and there's a socket mode. we'll include instructions for Node and Python. for throughput please provide expected tokens per request.
07:26 Speaker 4 (Samir): sample payloads coming — yes we'll send typical payloads (200-400 tokens) and expected rate 250 QPS for peak.
07:33 Speaker 1 (Maya): noted. that QPS suggests we might recommend a small dedicated pool for the pilot to get representative p95. we'll size and estimate cost.
07:45 Speaker 6 (Priya): question on latency SLOs — do you provide SLO alerting?
07:49 Speaker 2 (Ethan): Console has per-route latency dashboards and alerting hooks; we can hook to PagerDuty.
08:00 Speaker 5 (Jules): about data at rest: KMS integration means keys in our account?
08:04 Speaker 1 (Maya): with Private you can bring-your-own-KMS; with hosted we support customer-managed keys (CMK) with appropriate trust, we'll send the exact flow.
08:16 Speaker 3 (Laura): CI snippet for rotation?
08:19 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, here's an outline — store encrypted service token in Github secrets encrypted with your KMS, workflow decrypts and writes to REDWOOD_API_KEY env var, after rotation we call Redwood API to rotate the underlying service token. we'll share a sample GHA job.
08:38 Speaker 2 (Ethan): switching gears — orchestration question: do you have SDK-level retries and idempotency?
08:44 Speaker 3 (Laura): retries are critical for our workflow.
08:47 Speaker 2 (Ethan): SDK has configurable retries and idempotency keys. we also support client-side request ids so in logs you can trace the whole request through the runtime.
09:05 Speaker 4 (Samir): for our security review we'll need a short architecture diagram and a point of contact for penetration test coordination.
09:12 Speaker 1 (Maya): Ethan will be the technical contact; we'll attach a diagram and schedule a sync with your security team.
09:20 Speaker 5 (Jules): timeline — we want to be able to start a 2-week pilot next week.
09:24 Speaker 1 (Maya): we can start sandbox sooner; pilot with dedicated sizing needs about 3 business days.
09:31 Speaker 6 (Priya): does the SDK support telemetry events to our own analytics?
09:35 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes you can hook request-level webhooks and export traces to OTLP; we have a plugin for Datadog and Sumo as well.
09:46 Speaker 3 (Laura): any known issues with Node 20 or Python 3.11?
09:50 Speaker 2 (Ethan): supported — we maintain compatibility with Node 16+ and Python 3.8+. we'll include the compatibility matrix.
10:05 Speaker 1 (Maya): quick recap — action items and next steps, we'll share sandbox, SOC2 + KMS notes, and a pricing estimate for the dedicated pilot.
10:16 Speaker 3 (Laura): thanks everyone. one last thing — do you support EMR/offline batch workloads if we later need to rerun scoring?
10:22 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes, batching/batch transform jobs are supported via our batch API; not the same runtime as realtime but good for reprocessing.
10:30 Speaker 5 (Jules): ok that's helpful.
10:34 Speaker 1 (Maya): great, we'll follow up with an email and the artifacts. thanks for your time.

End of meeting.
